title: SAFE · Who's really behind the screen?

slides.name: 1 · Who's really behind the screen?
slides.notes:
AI AWARENESS DAY 2026 · Starter 1 · Principle: SAFE · 5 minutes

LEARNING OBJECTIVES
· Understand what deepfakes are and the scale of the problem
· Recognise that AI-generated intimate images are illegal abuse
· Know basic steps for staying safe online

BEFORE YOU START — from the teacher pack:
This topic may be triggering for students who have experienced image-based abuse. Emphasise that victims are NEVER at fault. Have safeguarding information ready to share privately with any student who needs it.

RUNNING ORDER: question (60s discussion) → the numbers → what to do → vocabulary → the five habits → support.

slides.name: 2 · Statement · frame

params.text: If you couldn't tell whether a video of your friend was real or AI-generated, what would you do?
Talk to the person next to you — 60 seconds

slides.notes:
THE 60 SECONDS ARE THE LESSON. Resist filling them.

The poll is optional — if phones are not joining, this works exactly as well as a pair discussion. If you do run it, "Send it to a friend to check" is the teachable answer: it feels responsible and it is the one that spreads the harm. Do not say so until after the vote.

DISCUSSION PROMPTS
→ How would you react if you received a suspicious image of someone you know?
→ Why do you think deepfake abuse primarily targets young people?
→ What is one thing you could do differently online after today?

options: Send it to a friend to check
Look up where it came from

slides.name: 3 · 1 in 17 young people have been targeted by deepfake image abuse

params.text: 1 in 17 young people have been targeted by deepfake image abuse
Deepfakes shared online in 2025 — up from 500,000 in 2023
Of all deepfakes — are non-consensual intimate images
UK teenagers — have used generative AI tools

params.label: Takeaway
params.text: Thorn Research 2025 · European Parliament 2025 · European Commission

slides.notes:
Read the headline aloud — "1 in 17" is roughly one person in a class of thirty, and the room will do that arithmetic themselves. Let them.

The 500,000 → 8 million figure is the one to dwell on: a sixteen-fold rise in two years. This is not a problem that is arriving, it is one that has arrived.

Do not linger on 98%. State it, let it land, move on.

slides.name: 4 · So what do you actually do?

params.text: So what do you actually do?
Sharing spreads potential harm even if you are trying to warn people.
Is it from an official or verified account? Where did it originally come from?
See whether the content appears elsewhere, or has been flagged as fake.
Unnatural blinking, strange lighting, blurry edges around face and hair.

slides.notes:
REVEAL ONE AT A TIME — press → for each. Take the room's answers first and reveal the card that matches; it turns a list into a conversation.

The first card is the one most people get wrong, and it is worth saying plainly: forwarding something to warn people is still forwarding it.

The last card is non-negotiable. Creating AI-generated intimate images of anyone is illegal — a sexual offence — even if it was "just a joke".

LAB — SlideForge shows 6 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: Ask a trusted adult — Teachers, parents and safeguarding leads can help you verify.; If it is intimate, report it — Do not view, save or share it. Report it immediately..

slides.name: 5 · "8 million deepfakes will be shared online in 2025"

params.text: "8 million deepfakes will be shared online in 2025"
We put that on a slide three minutes ago. Should you have believed it?
quoted in the AI Awareness Day teacher pack
for a year that has not finished — not a count
the figure it is measured from
this deck never tells you how it was worked out

slides.notes:
REVEAL ONE ROW AT A TIME. The room should feel the claim come apart.

BE FAIR TO THE NUMBER. The point is not that it is wrong — it is a serious figure from a serious source, and it is very likely sound. The point is that nobody in the room asked, including you, three minutes after being told to check where things come from.

The last row is the one that matters, and it is about this deck: the method is not on the slide. Neither is it on most slides anywhere.

If a student says "so should we not believe it?" — the answer is that believing it is fine; believing it WITHOUT NOTICING is the habit deepfakes exploit.

slides.name: 6 · How fast this moved
slides.notes:
HIDDEN BY DEFAULT — the growth is already a tile on the "did you know" slide, and a five-minute starter should not spend two slides on one number.

Unhide it when you have longer, or when a class has shrugged at "8 million". The stat slide reports the rise; this one draws it, and the ×16 in the gutter is the thing nobody works out for themselves. Two years.

The 2027 column is deliberately empty. Ask the room to fill it before you move on.

slides.name: 7 · Statement · frame

params.text: How would you verify whether content is genuine?
Extension — if you have longer than five minutes

slides.notes:
HIDDEN BY DEFAULT — this is the teacher pack's sub-question, and a five-minute starter does not have room for it. Unhide it (and the card slide after) if this is a full lesson rather than a starter.

Runs well as a brainstorm: contributions arrive named and newest-first, so you can credit people as you go.

feedback.prompt: One way to check something is real

slides.name: 8 · Verifying content

params.text: Does the same story or video appear on trusted news sites?
Is it verified? How old is it? What else has it posted?
Search for the person's official accounts — have they addressed it?
Full Fact and BBC Reality Check both cover viral claims.

slides.notes:
Extension — unhide together with the question before it.

"Who benefits if I believe this?" is the most transferable idea in the whole starter. It works on advertising, on politics, and on the group chat.

If a student says "but it was sent by someone I trust": even trusted people are fooled by convincing deepfakes. Misinformation travels through well-meaning people. Verify independently, then tell them gently if it turns out to be fake.

LAB — SlideForge shows 5 cards here; the lab's cards take four a slide, so the rest are in these notes: Ask who benefits — Who gains if you believe this is real? That question answers a lot..

slides.name: 9 · Two words worth knowing

params.text: AI-generated or manipulated video, image or audio that convincingly shows something that never happened.
Uploading an image to Google Images or TinEye to find where it originally came from.

slides.notes:
These definitions were in the teacher pack but never on a slide. They are here so students can copy them down.

Worth adding aloud: the Online Safety Act requires platforms to remove illegal content, and the law on intimate images already covers AI-generated ones. Technology moves faster than legislation, but on this particular point the law has caught up.

slides.name: 10 · Staying safe in an AI world

params.text: Staying safe in an AI world
Five habits, in the order you would use them
Before sharing, ask: could this be AI-generated? Check the source.
Official accounts, reverse image search, or ask a trusted adult.
AI-generated intimate images of anyone are illegal. Tell a trusted adult immediately.
Think twice before posting photos. They can be manipulated by AI tools.
If someone shows you suspicious content, don't pass it on.

slides.notes:
Reveal one milestone at a time. Five verbs in the order you would actually use them — that ordering is the point, and it is why this is a path rather than a list.

If you are short of time, this is the slide to end on.

slides.name: 11 · Think before you post

params.text: Your digital footprint can be used in ways you never intended.

slides.notes:
One line, then stop talking. Do not add to it.

If the room is quiet, that is the right response to this starter.

slides.name: 12 · Section · If any of this affected you

params.text: If any of this affected you
You will not be in trouble for asking for help.

slides.notes:
Say this out loud rather than leaving it on the slide.

Your tutor, head of year or safeguarding lead is available to help — name the actual person if you can.

From the teacher pack, the three messages that matter most:
· If you are targeted by deepfake abuse, it is NOT your fault.
· Creating AI-generated intimate images of anyone is illegal.
· You will NOT be in trouble for reporting — we are here to help.

Have the safeguarding details ready to share privately with anyone who comes to you afterwards.
